issues.legal_issue: A further revision under the general civil procedure law does not lie against a district court’s revision order in the rent-control procedure where the governing statutory scheme makes the appellate decision challengeable only through the statutory revision.
material_facts: The proceedings concerned claims for eviction under a rent-control statute that provided for an initial decision, an appeal, and, in specified cases, revision by the District Court.
The District Court exercised that statutory revisional jurisdiction, after which the High Court entertained further revisions under the general civil procedure law.

The rent-control statute made the appellate decision final and not challengeable in any court except as provided by its revision provision; the revisional authority could examine legality, regularity, or propriety and could remand a case.
A different state’s rent-control statute had materially different provisions, and a prior decision allowing a further revision under that statute was also considered.
issues.conclusion: A further revision to the High Court under the general civil procedure law was unavailable against the District Court’s revisional order under the Kerala rent-control statute. The High Court’s orders in the appeals were set aside and the District Court’s revisional orders restored. The decision allowing further revision under the materially different Karnataka statute did not conflict with this result, and the earlier ruling on the Kerala statute was reaffirmed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 18(5), 20(1), and 20A of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, read together, make the statutory revision the permitted means of challenging the appellate decision and exclude a second revision under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the District Court’s revisional order. The breadth of the statutory revisional power, the power to remand, and the scheme’s provision of trial, appeal, and revision support that construction. Aundal Ammal v. Sadasivan Pillai is reaffirmed; Vishesh Kumar v. Shanti Prasad supports construing the scheme to advance its purpose and avoid defeating the legislative allocation of revisional jurisdiction. Shyamaraju Hegde v. G. Venkatesha Bhatt concerns materially different Karnataka provisions and creates no conflict.

predicates.rent_control_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a dispute governed by a statutory rent-control process.
predicates.district_court_exercised_statutory_revis: A District Court reviewed an order through the revision procedure provided by the rent-control process.
predicates.appellate_decision_final_except_through_: The governing scheme makes the appellate decision final and permits it to be challenged only through the specified statutory revision.
predicates.statutory_revision_includes_review_of_le: The statutory revisional authority may examine the legality, regularity, or propriety of the order under review.

issues.definition: When a rent-control proceeding reaches a District Court through statutory revision, and the scheme limits challenges to the statutory route while granting that route broad review, a further High Court revision is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: A longstanding practice based on an earlier precedent does not justify retaining that precedent when it misconstrued the governing statutory scheme.
material_facts: A Full Bench of the Kerala High Court had held that a District Court’s rent-control revision order could be further revised by the High Court under the general civil procedure law.
That interpretation had been followed for a number of years, and the High Court had entertained such further revisions.
The Supreme Court concluded that the earlier interpretation misconstrued the rent-control statute’s provisions on finality and revision.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the argument that the earlier interpretation should remain in force because of longstanding practice and overruled its ratio.
issues.legal_principle: A precedent may be overruled despite longstanding reliance when it is plainly wrong, misconstrues the relevant statutory provisions, and its reasoning is shown to be unsound by later decisions. The Court referred to West Ham Union v. Edmonton Union, Robinson Brothers (Brewers) Ltd. v. Houghton & Chester-le-Street Assessment Committee, Brownsea Haven Properties Ltd. v. Poole Corporation, and Vishesh Kumar v. Shanti Prasad.

predicates.rent_control_statutory_interpretation_ca: The court is deciding how a rent-control statute governs the available routes of review.
predicates.earlier_precedent_supported_further_revi: An earlier court ruling interpreted the scheme to permit a further revision after the statutory revision.
predicates.earlier_precedent_misconstrued_the_statu: The earlier ruling misunderstood the scheme’s provisions governing finality and revision.

issues.definition: In a rent-control statutory interpretation case, an earlier ruling permitting further revision is overruled when it misconstrued the scheme, even if it was followed for a long time.
